name: Sémillon

lines.s10: Sémillon is the waxy, lemony grape behind golden Sauternes, and in Australia it makes a lean white that ages to toast and honey.
lines.s20: Sémillon is Bordeaux's golden grape, the heart of sweet Sauternes and the body in dry white Bordeaux. It tastes of lemon, green apple and beeswax, and when it is made sweet or aged for years it turns to honey, apricot and toast.
lines.s45: Sémillon leads two lives. In Bordeaux it is the golden grape of Sauternes, where a mould called noble rot shrivels the berries and leaves a sweet wine of honey, apricot and saffron. It is also the body in dry white Bordeaux, beside Sauvignon Blanc. Young and dry it tastes of lemon and beeswax, soft and rounded. Bordeaux often raises it in barrel, while Australia's Hunter Valley picks it early, uses no oak and waits. Pour the dry wines with shellfish or roast chicken, and Sauternes with blue cheese. After ten years a Hunter wine tastes of toast and honey, and it has never touched a barrel.
lines.sale: Sémillon gives a white with texture: lemon and beeswax when young, toast and honey with age. I would pour a dry one with the crab or the roast chicken, and a glass of Sauternes with the cheese.

glass.lead: Lemon, beeswax and lanolin when young and dry, turning to honey, apricot and toast with age or noble rot.

ladder.where: Bordeaux: Sauternes, Barsac, Graves and Pessac-Léognan; Margaret River
The Hunter Valley, picked early to stay lean; the Barossa, riper

glass.structure: Dry to lusciously sweet. Acidity medium in Bordeaux and high in young Hunter wines, alcohol low in the Hunter to high in Sauternes, body light to full.

old.where: Bordeaux: Sauternes and Barsac for sweet, Graves and Pessac-Léognan for dry
old.glass: Tends to be broad and waxy: lemon, beeswax and lanolin with gentle acidity, usually blended with Sauvignon Blanc. As Sauternes it is lusciously sweet, with honey, apricot and saffron on a full body.
old.cellar: Usually blended with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle; fermented and aged in barrel, some of it new, for the classed dry whites and for Sauternes.

new.where: Australia's Hunter Valley, Barossa and Margaret River; Franschhoek in South Africa
new.glass: Hunter Valley wines are typically light and bone dry when young, with lime, green apple and searing acidity at low alcohol; with a decade in bottle they turn to toast and honey. The Barossa tends to be riper and fuller.
new.cellar: In the Hunter it is picked early, fermented cold in steel and bottled young with no oak; Margaret River blends it with Sauvignon Blanc.

contrast.why: Bordeaux's misty autumns bring noble rot, and its tradition is the blend and the barrel. The Hunter is warm and humid, so growers pick early for acidity and let the bottle, not oak, do the ageing.
contrast.blur: Margaret River blends it with Sauvignon Blanc as Bordeaux does, the Riverina makes sweet wines from noble rot, and everyday white Bordeaux is often fresh and unoaked.
contrast.call: Wax, lanolin and vanilla from barrels, in a blend, lean Bordeaux; lime, searing acidity and low alcohol, or toast with no oak, lean Hunter Valley.

service.temp: Dry wines at 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius, barrel aged ones warmer; Sauternes colder.
service.glass: A white wine glass for dry wines; a small glass for Sauternes, poured two to three ounces.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; an old bottle of either style is simply poured with care.
service.age: Hunter Valley wines keep ten to twenty years or more, Sauternes for decades; most dry blends within five.

with.why: a waxy, rounded white for sweet shellfish
body to match the bird, lemon to echo

with.dish: Foie gras or chicken liver pâté
with.why: with Sauternes: sweetness and acidity cut the fat

labels.means: Sweet white Bordeaux from grapes shrivelled by noble rot; Sémillon leads the blend.
Dry white Bordeaux: Sémillon blended with Sauvignon Blanc, often fermented in barrel.
Australia's lean, unoaked, low alcohol style, built to age in bottle; spelt there without the accent.
A dry blend in the Bordeaux manner, made above all in Margaret River.

guest.a: Mostly, yes. Sémillon leads the blend, with Sauvignon Blanc and sometimes a little Muscadelle. Its thin skins welcome noble rot, the mould that shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar.

guest.q: Why does this old Australian Semillon taste toasty if it was never in oak?
guest.a: That is bottle age. Hunter Valley Semillon is picked early and made in steel, and after years in the bottle it develops toast and honey of its own accord.

guest.q: What does Sémillon add to white Bordeaux?
guest.a: Body and texture. Sauvignon Blanc brings the sharp, grassy lift, and Sémillon rounds it out with a waxy feel and the capacity to age.

compare.tell: Sauvignon Blanc is greener and louder, with cut grass, gooseberry and sharper acidity; Sémillon is broader and waxier, with lemon and lanolin.
Chenin Blanc is waxy too, but higher in acidity, with quince and baked apple; Sémillon is softer, with lemon, and toast as it ages.
Aged Riesling brings petrol and lime where aged Hunter Valley Sémillon brings toast and honey, and Riesling is the more perfumed when young.

cards.front: Sémillon: why is it the grape of Sauternes?
cards.back: Its thin skins and tight bunches welcome noble rot, which shrivels the berries and concentrates sugar. It leads the blend, with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle.

cards.front: Sémillon blind: Bordeaux or the Hunter Valley, what tips it?
cards.back: Wax, lanolin and vanilla from barrels, in a blend with Sauvignon Blanc, lean Bordeaux. Lime, searing acidity and low alcohol, or toast with no oak at all, lean Hunter Valley.

cards.front: Hunter Valley Sémillon: how is it made, and what does age bring?
cards.back: Picked early at low sugar, fermented cold in steel and bottled young with no oak. After five to ten years in bottle it gains toast and honey.

questions.q: A blind white is ten years old, deep lemon, bone dry and light, at low alcohol, with lime, toast and honey, high acidity and no vanilla at all. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Toast and honey with no barrel note, high acidity and low alcohol in an aged dry white is Hunter Valley Sémillon. Pessac-Léognan would be fuller, with vanilla from barrels, and Sauternes is sweet.

questions.q: A guest finishing dinner asks for the classic sweet wine of Bordeaux to go with Roquefort. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Sauternes is the sweet white of Bordeaux, led by Sémillon touched by noble rot, and a classic partner for Roquefort. Vouvray moelleux is Loire Chenin Blanc, and Tokaji Aszú is Hungarian.

questions.q: A dry white Bordeaux blends two main grapes. The Sauvignon Blanc brings sharp, grassy lift. What does the Sémillon bring?
opts: Body, a waxy texture and the capacity to age
A perfume of lychee and rose petal
High acidity and a light, lean frame
questions.exp: Sémillon gives white Bordeaux its body, its waxy texture and much of its capacity to age. High acidity and a lean frame are what the Sauvignon Blanc supplies.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it and as TASTE.world, both, requires: Bordeaux against Australia's Hunter Valley.

TASTE.age reads Hunter Semillon is famously immortal: an overstatement, though true in spirit. The entry says ten to twenty years or more, in line with Wine Australia, which says well over twenty for some.
The ladder has no cool rung: the Hunter is warm and humid and keeps its lean, lime and green apple style by early picking, which the rung says in its place.
The Barossa is described only as riper and fuller: Wine Australia says barrel fermented and aged wines are richer but does not tie that style to the Barossa in the pages read.
Franschhoek stands on the Codex's own region records. No Creole dish is given: none of the seven truly suits better than the dishes listed.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The thin skins and tight bunches, the Hunter Valley style and its ageing, and the Barossa were confirmed.
changed: lines.s20: lanolin, a word a guest would need explained, gives way to green apple. The glass and the Old World side keep it.
worlds.contrast.blur: the Riverina's sweet wines made by noble rot are named, the New World's own answer to Sauternes and the exception the line lacked.
service.temp: barrel aged dry wines are served warmer, as the Sauvignon Blanc entry and the Codex's row for full whites have it.
